White-tailed ptarmigan (Lagopus leucura) chicks emerge from eggs incubated at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with hatching typically occurring after 23 days [ab = 23 days], though the incubation period can range between 22 and 24 days under natural conditions. At the moment of hatching, these precocial young exhibit a wet weight at birth of 12.9 grams [Wwb = 12.9 grams], a value that reflects the substantial yolk reserves allocated to each egg. This initial mass is notably modest when compared to the adult dimensions the birds will eventually achieve. The developmental trajectory is rapid; fledging, defined as the achievement of first sustained flight, occurs at just 9 days after hatching [tx = 9 days after hatching]. This early flight capability is a critical adaptation for evading predators in the exposed alpine tundra habitats the species occupies. The brief nestling period is characterized by intense parental brooding and foraging, as the downy chicks must quickly thermoregulate and begin feeding independently. Given the abbreviated time in the nest, the investment per egg is considerable, setting the stage for a life history strategy that balances high offspring quality against environmental constraints on reproductive output.

Reproductive output in this species is typically limited to a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], with females laying between 4 and 16 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 4 and 16 eggs per clutch]. This clutch size is highly variable and likely reflects local resource availability and female body condition at the time of laying. The single-brooded strategy is common among high-elevation galliforms, where the brief summer window constrains opportunities for renesting. The resulting maximum annual reproductive rate is modest, a pattern consistent with a slow-paced life history adapted to cold, resource-limited environments. Females invest heavily in each clutch, and the eggs are large relative to body size, providing the developing embryo with sufficient nutrients to hatch as a well-developed, mobile chick. The cost of this investment is balanced by a long potential lifespan, which allows individuals multiple breeding seasons over their lifetime. Field studies suggest that not all females breed every year, particularly following harsh winters, which further tempers the population-level reproductive contribution.

The mass trajectory from hatchling to adult is striking. The initial wet weight of a newly hatched chick is 20 grams [Ww0 = 20 grams], a value derived from the 12.9 gram birth mass plus the absorption of residual yolk and initial feeding. From this modest starting point, chicks undergo a period of accelerated growth during the first few weeks of life. Adult body mass is sexually dimorphic; males ultimately reach a wet weight of 359 grams [Wwi = 359 grams], while females attain a slightly lower ultimate wet weight of 351 grams [Wwi = 351 grams]. This dimorphism is typical among ptarmigan species and is thought to be related to sexual selection on male body size for territorial defense and female choice. The nearly 18-fold increase in mass from hatching to adulthood is fueled by a diet of alpine plant buds, leaves, and insects during the summer months. The rapid accumulation of tissue is particularly important before the onset of winter, when food availability plummets and energy demands for thermoregulation soar. This growth trajectory is closely tied to the species' high-latitude, high-elevation distribution.

Sexual maturation in White-tailed ptarmigan follows a predictable developmental schedule. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, occurs at 27 days after hatching [tp = 27 days after hatching], though some sources indicate this milestone can be reached as early as 7 to 10 days after hatching. This early physiological capability for gamete production is not immediately translated into reproductive behavior. First reproduction is typically deferred until the individual is significantly older, with females initiating breeding at 545 days after hatching [tR = 545 days after hatching] and males sometimes as early as 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching]. The delay between puberty and first breeding is a common life-history pattern in long-lived birds, allowing young birds to gain body mass, establish territories, and acquire the foraging experience necessary to successfully incubate a clutch and care for young. This deferred breeding strategy likely enhances lifetime reproductive success by reducing the mortality risk associated with inexperienced early breeding attempts in a harsh alpine environment.

Longevity records for wild White-tailed ptarmigan indicate a maximum lifespan of 5475 days [am = 5475 days], which equates to approximately 15 years. This considerable lifespan, rare among small-bodied galliforms, is a hallmark of a slow life-history strategy adapted to stable, low-mortality environments. The oldest documented individuals are typically those that successfully navigate the extreme seasonal challenges of the alpine zone, including deep snow cover, limited forage, and intense predation pressure from raptors and mammals. Given this extended lifespan, even the modest annual reproductive output of a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] can result in substantial lifetime fecundity when combined with high adult survival. The trade-off between current reproduction and future survival is a central axis of the species' life history, with individuals likely prioritizing their own maintenance during harsh years at the expense of breeding. Comparative data from congeneric species such as the rock ptarmigan (Lagopus muta) suggest similar longevity patterns, reinforcing the view that the Lagopus genus has converged on a slow-paced, high-survival life-history strategy in cold climates.
